title: Classes & Objects
description: Bundle data and behavior together with classes — define your own types and give them methods that act on their own state.
objectives: Define a class with `__init__` and instance methods
Set and read instance attributes via `self`
Recognize when a class is the right shape — and when a function or dict is enough
recap: A class is a blueprint for objects: `__init__` runs at construction time and stashes data on `self` (the instance); methods are functions that take `self` as their first argument so they can read and modify that data. Reach for a class when you have data + behavior that travel together. If you only have data, a dict or a tuple is often simpler.
practicePrompts: Look at a function from earlier in the course that takes the same first argument over and over. Could that argument be `self` on a class? Would the call sites read better?
When is a `dict` clearer than a class? Think about what each makes easy and what each makes hard.

practiceExercises.title: A counter class
practiceExercises.prompt:
Define a class `Counter` with these features:
- `__init__(self, start=0)` stores `start` as `self.value`.
- `increment(self)` increases `self.value` by 1.
- `reset(self)` sets `self.value` back to 0.

For example, `Counter().value` is `0`, `Counter(5).value` is `5`. After calling `c.increment()` twice on a fresh `Counter()`, `c.value` should be `2`.
practiceExercises.goal: Write a class with a constructor and two state-mutating methods.
hints: Each instance needs its own `value`, set when the object is created. That's what `__init__` is for.
Inside a method, use `self.value` to read or write the attribute. `__init__` sets it once; `increment` and `reset` change it.

practiceExercises.title: A greeter class
practiceExercises.prompt:
Define a class `Greeter` with:
- `__init__(self, name)` stores `name` on `self.name`.
- `greet(self)` returns the string `"Hello, <name>!"`.

For example, `Greeter("Alice").greet()` should return `"Hello, Alice!"`.
practiceExercises.goal: Use an instance attribute to compose a return value from a method.
hints: Two parts: stash the name in `__init__`, then build the greeting in `greet` using that stored name.
In `__init__`, write `self.name = name`. In `greet`, return an f-string that interpolates `self.name` between `"Hello, "` and `"!"`.

practiceExercises.title: A LIFO stack
practiceExercises.prompt:
Define a class `Stack` (last-in-first-out) with:
- `__init__(self)` creates an empty list `self.items`.
- `push(self, item)` appends `item` to `self.items`.
- `pop(self)` removes and returns the last item.
- `peek(self)` returns the last item without removing it.

For example, after `s = Stack(); s.push(1); s.push(2)`, `s.peek()` returns `2` and `s.pop()` returns `2`. After the pop, `s.peek()` returns `1`.
practiceExercises.goal: Combine a list-typed attribute with multiple methods that work over it.

tests.name: items list state
tests.setup:
s = Stack()
s.push('a')
s.push('b')
s.push('c')
s.pop()

hints: A stack is just a list with a fixed access pattern: you only ever look at, add to, or remove from the end. Lists already have `.append` and `.pop` for those.
